name: Bianca Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, parties or government. What you say is confidential. Tell me about a usual day at work.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27 and I lead the later shift at a contact centre. I've got a two-year college diploma, and I've learned to hear when a customer is about to give up on us. I answer calls and chats, keep a paper log of refunds that need another look, and make sure the new agents don't rush a caller off the line.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What feels good about that, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A customer who calls back to say the charge was fixed can make my day. The timer on my screen wears me down. I earn less than most leads, and there's not even a full month's bills saved if my shifts change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the phones will still ring and customers will still want a clear answer. A small shortcut on routine messages won't change the point of our desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I believe that, but the centre already watches every minute we spend after a call. I'm good at this job, yet my wages are low for a lead and my savings don't cover a month's bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep my paper log of difficult refunds and ask for my usual shifts each month. From now through the first year of a plateau, I'll stop replacing my worn phone and put what I can into a bill envelope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more settled about the job than about the money. One bad rota can undo a careful month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What purchase would you delay first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The phone still works, even with a cracked corner. Buying another would empty the little I have set aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your family cover a missed shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father sometimes offers money, but I don't want to build ordinary rent around his help. I'd ask only if my shifts were cut and the rent was due.

say: I'd say **customers** still need clear answers from our desk.
I'd expect only **small shortcuts** on routine messages.
think: I see the centre watch **every minute** after calls.
My **low pay** and tiny cushion make lost shifts dangerous.
do: Keep a **paper log** of difficult refunds.
Ask for **usual shifts** on each monthly rota.
Delay replacing my **worn phone** to protect bill money.
feel: **Job relief** is tempered by worry about the rota.
S0.quote: One bad rota can undo a careful month.
fieldNote: She trusts her **call skills** more than new software.
Her **money worry** predates any major AI change.
She delays a **phone purchase** to protect money for ordinary bills.

steps.text: Keep a paper log of difficult customer refunds
Put spare pay into a bill envelope

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team that easy chats disappearing will leave us with angry people and fewer breaks. Management should say plainly whether shifts will be lost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the company will call it efficiency and expect one lead to cover two queues. I know the work better than most, but there are few similar jobs in town if my hours go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask for a written rota forecast at the next staff meeting and keep taking the hard calls. If hours fall in the first year, I'll cut my bus trips to weekend visits and ask my supervisor for paid extra shifts before looking outside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious. My skill counts, but it doesn't pay a bill if they take hours off the rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you take to the meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring last month's call figures and ask what staffing number management actually plans. I won't sign up for a course just because a screen tells me to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you look if hours fell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd first ask at the centre for paid hours, not a promise of a future post. If there are no hours, I would ask the pharmacy down the road whether its desk has a paid opening.

say: I'd demand a **rota forecast** before easy chats vanish.
I'd warn that **hard calls** will fill the remaining queue.
think: I fear management may make one **lead cover two queues** while presenting fewer shifts as ordinary efficiency.
do: Request a **written forecast** at the next staff meeting.
Ask for **paid extra shifts** if hours fall.
Check the **pharmacy desk** only if a paid opening exists.
feel: **Anxiety** comes from possible lost hours despite strong skills.
S1.quote: My skill counts, but it doesn't pay a bill if they take hours off the rota.
fieldNote: She seeks **written staffing numbers** before acting.
Her possible **job search** starts locally and requires paid work.
She would **cut travel** before relying on help from family.

steps.text: Keep handling difficult customer calls while hours remain
Ask the nearby pharmacy about a paid desk vacancy
Cut bus trips for weekend visits if shifts fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the centre owes people straight notice if general AI can answer the calls by 2028. Robots around 2031 don't delay what happens to our headsets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my lead role could disappear, and I don't have the savings to sit out even a month. I'm proud of doing the job properly; that won't make a cheaper system wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomorrow I'll gather my contract, pay slips and rota records, then ask what notice and paid vacancies the company would offer. If my role goes in the first year after 2028, I'll apply for paid reception work at the clinic and ask my father about temporary help only if the rent comes due first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel almost cornered. I can make calls and collect papers, but two years isn't much time to build money from this wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much family help could you ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my father for one month's rent at most, and only after showing him the layoff letter. I couldn't ask him to carry me without an end date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your supervisor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A machine can answer a question, but a dismissal still needs a human face. I want the notice terms in writing, not whispered across the floor.

say: I'd demand **straight notice** if general AI removes call roles.
I'd point out **2031 robots** do not delay headset work changing.
think: My **lead role** could disappear by 2028 because calls and chats are thinking work.
My savings below **one month** cannot cover a long search.
do: Gather my **contract and rota** records tomorrow.
Seek a **paid clinic vacancy** after an actual job loss.
Ask my **father** for one month’s rent only after layoff if rent falls due first.
feel: **Alarm** comes from a short deadline and no financial cushion.
S2.quote: A machine can answer a question, but a dismissal still needs a human face.
fieldNote: Her **pride in craft** cannot reassure her about a cheaper replacement.
She views **family help** as bounded and conditional.
She wants **notice terms** documented before any cut.

steps.text: Apply for paid clinic reception vacancies if laid off
Ask father for one month's rent after layoff if rent falls due first

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell people five years is time to insist on a proper handover, not a last-minute message on the noticeboard. The calls still face general AI in 2031, before any robots in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might be able to move into reception or complaints work while I'm still employed. I don't trust a promised new role without a posted vacancy and a wage I can live on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this year, I'll ask the clinic what its reception work pays and keep a folder of the complex cases I settled. If a paid vacancy opens before 2031, I'll apply; in the first year after AGI arrives, I'll stay at the centre while shifts exist and search again if they shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm worried but less trapped. Five years lets me learn the other desk without betting my rent on a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you learn about clinic reception?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could visit the clinic on a day off and ask the desk manager what experience is required. I won't take unpaid trial shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI to impress a new employer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I wouldn't use AI in my own calls just to prove I'm modern. I'd rather show a real complaint record and listen to what the clinic needs.

say: I'd ask for a **proper handover** before call jobs shrink.
I'd say **2034 robots** offer no delay for telephone work.
think: Five years may permit a **paid move** into reception while I still have wages from the centre.
I distrust **unposted roles** and vague wage promises.
do: Ask the **clinic desk** what reception pays this year.
Apply only for **posted paid vacancies** before or after 2031.
feel: **Worry** eases because she can investigate without resigning.
S3.quote: I won't take unpaid trial shifts.
fieldNote: Her **five-year plan** relies on checking real wages first.
She stays **technology resistant**, using her case record as proof of skill.
She rejects **unpaid trials** because they cannot cover rent or show a reliable wage.

steps.text: Ask the clinic desk manager about paid reception vacancies
Keep working contact centre shifts while they remain available

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade lets employers give proper notice and lets workers choose their next post. Our call work faces general AI in 2036; the 2039 robot date isn't the one to watch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could change jobs well before 2036 if the right paid opening appears. But I won't spend ten years worrying over a date while I need this month's wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the next year I'll keep my contact-centre role and put small spare amounts in the bill envelope. I'll check the clinic's posted wages twice a year, and in the first year after 2036 I'd apply only if there is a paid opening that covers my bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more grounded. A ten-year warning lets me stay careful without pretending my savings are fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What wage would make the move possible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need a wage at least equal to what I bring home now, even though that pay is low for a lead. A nicer title won't cover rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger cousin?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my younger cousin to choose work she can respect and to check the actual wage. I won't tell her every future job is doomed just because my desk may change.

say: I'd call for **proper notice** during the long transition.
I'd tell agents **2036 thinking AI** matters more to calls than 2039 robots.
think: I could make a **measured move** before 2036.
I still need this month's **wage** more than a distant promise.
do: Keep my **contact-centre role** through the coming year.
Put **spare pay** in the bill envelope.
Check **clinic wages** twice yearly; apply only for paid vacancies matching my current take-home pay.
feel: **Grounded** by time to choose without gambling rent.
S4.quote: A nicer title won't cover rent.
fieldNote: She holds to **familiar work** while it pays.
The **longer runway** lowers urgency but does not cure her thin savings.
She checks **posted wages** because a title without enough pay would worsen her position.

steps.text: Keep contact centre shifts through the coming year
Put spare pay into the monthly bill envelope
Check clinic vacancies twice yearly; apply only where pay matches current take-home

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because a two-year warning and less than a month's savings leave nowhere to stand. A written notice period, paid openings I can actually apply for, and a short bridge if shifts end would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who tells customers when a real person is gone from the line. I would hate for a customer to think a named agent had listened when nobody had. Honesty should count for something.

headlineQuote: I would hate for a customer to think a named agent had listened when nobody had.
portrait: Bianca is a **27-year-old lead** in a contact centre, skilled at resolving complaints and supporting new agents.
Her **two-year diploma** and strong performance coexist with low lead pay, savings below one month and few nearby alternatives.
She prefers **familiar methods**, avoids AI tools and asks for written terms before risking a change of job.
The **2028 picture** alarms her; longer warnings give her time to check real wages and paid clinic openings.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her role before she has money for even a month of job searching.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice** and posted paid vacancies would let her plan a move.
A short **income bridge** would help if shifts end before she finds work.
